about.en: The other side of the same hold: instead of trapping a leg you attack their head-side balance, bridging hard and rolling them over your own shoulder line. Higher grades in every scheme here examine both escapes.

en: Get onto your side before you bridge, not flat on your back
Bridge towards their head, over your own shoulder, not straight up
Follow them over; do not stop when they start to move
You are held in Kesa-gatame with your right arm trapped and their weight across your chest.
Reach your free left arm over their back and grip their belt or their far side to stop them posting away.
Turn onto your right side and pull yourself in tight to them, taking away the space they need.
Bridge sharply up and over your right shoulder, driving your hips towards their head rather than straight upwards.
As their weight goes past your shoulder, keep turning in the same direction and roll them over.
Finish on top or on your knees, and pull the trapped arm free once you are settled.

receiving.en: You will feel them tuck in tight and take a grip on your back before anything happens. The answer is to post your head-side arm out wide and lower your hips: a hold with a wide base and a low centre does not roll.

viNotes.en: The cue to bridge is contact, not sight: their body tight against yours with no gap. Feel for their belt with your free hand first, then commit. Roll in the direction your own shoulder is already pointing.
